title: Functions, arrow functions and this
idea: A function is reusable code stored as a value. Its `this` is decided by the call; an arrow function borrows `this` from the code around it.

analogy.text: `this` is like the word 'I': it means whoever speaks the sentence, not whoever wrote it. An arrow function is a sentence with the speaker already filled in.
analogy.breaks: A plain call has no speaker, so `this` is `undefined` in strict code.

points: Three common forms make a function: declaration, expression and arrow `=>`.
Regular functions take `this` from the call: the object before the dot.
`call` runs a function with a chosen `this`; `bind` returns a fixed copy.
An arrow function has no own `this`: it uses the one around it.

walk.text: A `class` is a template for objects. Inside its methods, `this` is the object the call used.
`new User('Ada')` makes `ada`. `ada.hello()` is a method call: `this` is `ada`, the object before the dot.
Calling the copied method `detached()` has no object before the dot. `this` is undefined, so `this.name` throws.
`bind(ada)` returns a new function whose `this` is fixed to `ada`.
`ada.reader()` returns an arrow. It has no own `this`, so it uses the `this` of `reader`: `ada`.

pitfalls: A method passed to another function loses `this`; wrap it in an arrow or `bind` it.
Do not use an arrow function as an object method: its `this` is not the object.
Arrow functions cannot be called with `new`; write constructors with `class`.

quiz.why: `user.hi()` sets `this` to `user`. `call(other)` runs the same function with `this` set to `other`.

takeaway: Calls set `this` for regular functions; arrows keep the `this` where they are written.
